title: Agentic AI Alters The CPU-GPU Balance
gist: Agentic AI adds if-then-else orchestration work that suits CPUs, so the CPU:GPU ratio in AI clusters may move from about 1:4 toward 1:1, tightening CPU supply and nudging prices up. Reasoning models, mixture-of-experts and reservoir computing remain GPU/accelerator-bound and broaden rather than consolidate the AI model landscape.

insights.claim: Agentic AI orchestrates models with decision-heavy if-then-else logic that suits CPUs rather than GPUs, so agentic workloads raise CPU demand inside AI clusters.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Watch CPU vendors and server CPU supply as a second-order beneficiary of the agent build-out.

insights.claim: According to some industry estimates, agentic workloads could shift the CPU-to-GPU ratio in AI systems from about 1:4 for typical LLMs to as low as 1:1.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: A move toward 1:1 would multiply CPU unit demand per GPU deployed; track CPU attach rates in server orders.
insights.quote: agentic workloads could alter the ratio of CPUs to GPUs from 1:4 to as low as 1:1

insights.claim: With typical LLMs the CPU mostly acts as a light-load host managing setup and PCIe communication for several GPUs, whereas with agents the CPU does actual work.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: CPU sizing assumptions built on host-only duty cycles will understate agentic-era requirements.

insights.claim: Higher CPU demand from agentic AI can nudge CPU prices upward, and a QCI executive says CPUs are getting very expensive right now.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: CPU supply tightness and pricing power are a monitorable signal for server CPU makers and server cost inflation.
insights.quote: This is why CPUs are getting very expensive right now.
insights.locator: In the last 18 months, everyone is clamoring over agentic AI

insights.claim: A single request to an agent typically triggers many model queries as the agent works through its series of tasks, making agentic inference more compute-intensive than a single-query LLM call.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Token and compute demand per user request grows with agent adoption, supporting infrastructure capex.
insights.locator: Agentic queries are also more compute-intensive

insights.claim: Delos Data's CEO cites new research saying agentic inference will dwarf all prior inference put together, and describes the CPU as back but used in a very different way than elsewhere in the data center.
insights.speaker: Ed Doe, CEO and co-founder of Delos Data (quoted by Bryon Moyer)
insights.so_what: If agentic inference becomes the dominant workload, infrastructure demand mix shifts toward CPU-plus-accelerator designs.
insights.quote: There is some new research out there that says agentic inference is going to dwarf everything else put together before it

insights.claim: Synopsys says the design question used to be how many AI accelerators could be attached per CPU, but with agentic AI the added CPU load has changed those ratios.
insights.speaker: Ron Lowman, Synopsys (quoted by Bryon Moyer)
insights.so_what: Platform architects and IP vendors are reorienting around higher CPU content per AI node.
insights.quote: With agentic AI, there's more CPU load demand, and therefore the ratios have changed.
insights.locator: The challenge used to be how many AI accelerators we can get per CPU

insights.claim: Agentic AI puts a premium on CPUs without removing any of the pressure on GPUs, making it the big exception among model types that otherwise rely mainly on GPUs or NPUs.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Agentic AI is additive to GPU demand and also adds CPU demand, so it is not a substitution trade.

insights.claim: An AI agent is a higher level of abstraction that orchestrates models rather than a model itself; it sends tokens to a model, decides what to do next based on the result, and acts without tight supervision.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Agents sit on top of existing models, so they add demand to the model and compute stack rather than replacing it.

insights.claim: Arm says agentic AI took off since last year and agents can take a high-level request, such as arranging a multi-day trip with a budget, and then call APIs to take action on the user's behalf.
insights.speaker: Satadal Bhattacharjee, Arm (quoted by Bryon Moyer)
insights.so_what: Consumer and enterprise agents that transact via APIs are the use case driving the infrastructure shift.
insights.locator: Since last year, agentic AI took off

insights.claim: Arm says demand for CPUs has risen a lot because everyone is looking for much more compute, in a power-efficient way, to run agents; agent sequencing can also be tuned with JSON scripts.
insights.speaker: Satadal Bhattacharjee, Arm (quoted by Bryon Moyer)
insights.so_what: Power-efficient CPU architectures are positioned to benefit from agent-driven demand.

insights.claim: Reasoning models spend additional inference compute, generating extra tokens and neural-network computation, which runs primarily on GPUs or other accelerators rather than CPUs.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Reasoning-model adoption raises accelerator inference demand, not CPU demand.

insights.claim: Reasoning models can give an accounting of how they reached an answer and can be retrained when a reasoning step was wrong, which helps address the difficulty of certifying opaque models for safety.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Explainability is a gating factor for safety-critical AI deployment and may favor reasoning-style models there.

insights.claim: Basic neural models have no deterministic way to trace their calculations and different random initializations train to different yet still correct models, which makes certifying safety-critical systems hard.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Certification burden is a structural obstacle for AI in regulated, safety-critical applications.

insights.claim: OpenAI's O-series models and DeepSeek-R1 are cited as commercially deployed reasoning models, though reasoning models are less widespread than LLMs and agentic AI.
insights.speaker: Satadal Bhattacharjee, Arm (quoted by Bryon Moyer)
insights.so_what: Reasoning inference is already commercial, adding to accelerator demand at the leading labs.
insights.quote: OpenAI's O-series models and DeepSeek-R1 are examples of commercially deployed reasoning models
insights.locator: Reasoning models have been commercially released

insights.claim: Mixture-of-experts models replace dense feed-forward layers with multiple expert FFNs and a learned router, so only one or two experts process each token and not all parameters need to be fetched.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Sparse activation lets model capacity grow faster than per-token compute and memory traffic.
insights.quote: That sparse activation is the key advantage.
insights.locator: An MoE model can have a very large total parameter count

insights.claim: Synopsys notes that MoE avoids needing a single 10-trillion-parameter model by splitting capacity into roughly 1-trillion-parameter experts for domains such as legal and math, with a front-end model routing the query.
insights.speaker: Priyank Shukla, Synopsys (quoted by Bryon Moyer)
insights.so_what: MoE changes the scaling path from raw parameter count to specialization and routing, shifting hardware needs.
insights.locator: Earlier we had this scaling in large language models

insights.claim: In an MoE model the KV cache holding the inference context must be transmitted from the first model to the selected expert, creating inter-device communication demand, while the router itself runs on the accelerator.
insights.speaker: Priyank Shukla, Synopsys (quoted by Bryon Moyer)
insights.so_what: MoE raises interconnect and memory-movement requirements, which favors interface IP and high-bandwidth links.
insights.quote: We have to transmit the KV cache from the first model, which interacts with the relevant mixture of experts
insights.locator: The context reflecting everything that's happened so far

insights.claim: MoE models use fewer computations per token than a dense model of comparable total parameter count, but routing, memory access and device-to-device communication add overhead, so efficiency depends on system design rather than parameter count.
insights.speaker: Satadal Bhattacharjee, Arm (quoted by Bryon Moyer)
insights.so_what: Power savings from MoE are not guaranteed; system-level design determines the benefit.
insights.locator: Less clear are the power implications of MoE models

insights.claim: Small language models handle whole token strings within a narrow specialty, while MoE experts handle only certain tokens in a string, and MoE models are larger than comparable dense models but smaller than a single model trained to cover everything without experts.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: SLMs suit narrow, resource-constrained deployments while MoE targets broad coverage at frontier scale.

insights.claim: Mixture-of-experts models are becoming very popular and gaining traction, enabling specialized queries that require fewer parameters to load.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: MoE is a mainstream architecture trend that hardware roadmaps need to support.

insights.claim: Reservoir computing handles time sequences with a mostly random model where only the last layer is trained, so most of the model can be hard-coded into silicon and only last-layer weights must be fetched, cutting energy use.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Reservoir computing is a niche low-power option for edge sequence tasks like speech, sensors and robot motor control.

insights.claim: Quantum Computing Inc. is readying a photonic reservoir computer, and QCI says photonics is among the best implementation choices because of bandwidth and can use wavelength-division multiplexing to run tasks in parallel.
insights.speaker: Prajnesh Kumar, QCI (quoted by Bryon Moyer)
insights.so_what: Watch QCI's launch as a test of commercial demand for photonic reservoir computing.
insights.quote: photonics is one of the best choices because of the bandwidth
insights.locator: Quantum Computing Inc. (QCI) has a photonic version

insights.claim: QCI names target applications for photonic reservoir computing including vertical-takeoff vehicle trajectory planning, brain-signal classification such as epilepsy, and military and defense uses.
insights.speaker: Prajnesh Kumar, QCI (quoted by Bryon Moyer)
insights.so_what: Early use cases are specialized and niche, so near-term revenue visibility is limited.
insights.locator: That way, they're addressing specific tasks

insights.claim: CNNs, LLMs, agentic AI, MoE, reasoning models and reservoir computing coexist, and the specialized approaches broaden the AI landscape rather than pointing to a single dominant architecture.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Hardware that targets a single model type carries architecture risk; flexible heterogeneous compute is favored.

insights.claim: Retrieval-augmented generation improved early LLMs by letting them access embeddings containing real facts, which reduced hallucinations that arose because the models only predicted a likely next word.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Factual grounding via retrieval is a baseline requirement for reliable enterprise LLM use.
